claim: The theory says the conformance suite tests calibration; the suite tests only shape.
evidence: THEORY.md:304: "That is the entire contract, and it is what the conformance suite tests — shapes and calibration, never a vendor's keys." lib/s1/rspec.rb examples: returns a Result; answers every id with the right class; probabilities in [0,1]; keys; scale; collapses; supports?; integer usage. README.md:986: "It checks the shape, not the wisdom". No example touches calibration.
proposal: Reword 304: "what the conformance suite tests is the shape; calibration is the provider's warranty and is not testable offline."
reasons: The claim holds. THEORY.md:154 defines calibration as an empirical frequency property ("a mass of 0.7 means that among such judgements, seven in ten are true"), which requires ground truth across many judgements; lib/s1/rspec.rb runs one fixed request against a stubbed client (spec/s1/conformance_spec.rb feeds hand-picked 0.8/0.6 numbers, and the Stub provider is passed its answers) and asserts only class, id/key sets, scale, [0,1] bounds, sum≈1, collapse type, supports?, and integer usage. The nearest candidate, "probabilities sum to 1", is normalization — that the distribution is a distribution — not calibration. README.md:986 ("It checks the shape, not the wisdom") states the opposite of THEORY.md:304 in the gem's own words, so this is a real text-vs-code-vs-README inconsistency with reader consequence: a provider author could believe passing the suite certifies calibration. The proposed reword is the correct direction; calibration is the provider's warranty, unverifiable offline.

Not refutable. THEORY.md:153 defines the bold term **Calibration** as "a mass of 0.7 means that among such judgements, seven in ten are true" — a frequency property over many judgements against ground truth — and under the theory's own bold-term discipline that is what "calibration" at line 304 must mean. lib/s1/rspec.rb's only probability example ("keeps probabilities as probabilities", lines 42-47) checks [0,1] and sum-within-0.02-of-1, i.e. normalization, and the shared examples are by their own header built to run against "a stubbed HTTP client, a fake sidecar" (lines 10-11), where fixed canned masses cannot be calibrated or miscalibrated at all; spec/s1/conformance_spec.rb and live_spec.rb add fidelity (0.7 in → 0.7 out) and range checks, never a calibration check. README.md:986 states the opposite of 304 outright ("It checks the shape, not the wisdom"), and the "where they disagree, the code is wrong" rule cannot rescue 304 because an offline suite cannot test calibration in principle, so the sentence, not the suite, is what must change. Reader consequence is real: a provider author reading 304 would take a green suite as certification of the axiom the whole pre-collapse arithmetic (line 156) rests on.

claim: Confidence is defined as distinct from the mass on the winning category, but the cua provider (which the theory claims to hold for) sets confidence = argmax mass.
evidence: THEORY.md:167-168: "the model's own estimate of how reliable a nominal or ordinal judgement is — distinct from the mass on the winning category." cua.rb:49: `pick, confidence = probabilities.max_by { |_, p| p }`. README.md:964: "the argmax is the pick and its probability the confidence".
proposal: Either define confidence as "a provider-reported reliability scalar; may coincide with the winning mass when the provider has no separate signal" or make Cua report nil (so confident? reads true and callers read confidence per line 171).
reasons: THEORY.md:167-168 defines confidence as "distinct from the mass on the winning category" and gives one carve-out only (nil when the provider reports none); cua.rb:49 sets confidence to exactly the winning mass, spec/s1/providers/cua_spec.rb:21 asserts `answer.confidence == answer.probabilities["phone"]`, and README.md:964-965 documents it as Cua's translation — so the theory and code plainly disagree, and by the theory's own rule the code is wrong. Nothing in THEORY.md addresses a provider that substitutes a proxy for a separate reliability signal; the only addressed case is nil. It is not taste-only: the normalized Distribution exists so "a second provider slots in unchanged" (distribution.rb:5-8), yet `confident?(at)` on Cua reduces to `probabilities.values.max >= at` while on jev it reads a shape-derived scalar, so the same gate at the same `at` means different things across the providers the theory claims to hold for, and a reader following line 171 would treat Cua's value as an independent signal it is not. The gem's own fixtures (Stub 1.0 on one-hot, conformance 0.8/0.6 equal to winning mass) show the "distinct" wording is not even honored as a norm, which strengthens rather than refutes the inconsistency. The claim stands; the definition needs the proposed provider-latitude wording or Cua needs to report nil.

Not refuted. THEORY.md:167-171 defines confidence as "distinct from the mass on the winning category" and prescribes the alternative for a provider with no separate signal: report nil, so `confident?(at)` reads true and callers "read `confidence` itself to escalate those." Cua does neither — lib/s1/providers/cua.rb:49 sets confidence to the argmax mass, README.md:965 documents that as the design, and spec/s1/providers/cua_spec.rb:21 pins it (`expect(answer.confidence).to eq(answer.probabilities["phone"])`), while THEORY.md:305 asserts cua-s1-forms is "an instance of the same arrow." The reader consequence is concrete: `confident?(at)` on a Cua choice is silently a threshold on winning mass, and the nil-escalation path the theory promises never fires for Cua, so a caller cannot distinguish a provider-reported reliability from a synthesized one. The "calibrated argmax mass is reliability" defense is foreclosed by the theory's own "distinct from" wording; by its own standard ("where they disagree, the code is wrong") either the text or Cua must change.

claim: In Rails a float column is called a collapse rule that "keeps the mass", but collapse is defined as the step after which nothing probabilistic survives.
evidence: 277-278: "the collapse rule is the column type — a boolean column collapses at the threshold, a float keeps the mass". 63-64: Category — "Nothing probabilistic survives." 296-297: "Writing the answer into the row is the collapse; keeping a JSON column beside it is keeping the distribution." A Bernoulli's mass is the whole distribution (46: "one number determines it"), so a float column is not a collapse.
proposal: Split the bullet: "the collapse rule is the column type — boolean at the threshold, enum/string the category, integer the level's rank; a float column is not a collapse but a sibling that keeps the mass."
reasons: Not refuted. THEORY.md:277-279 puts "a float keeps the mass" in the same list, with the same verb "keeps", as "keeps the category" and "keeps the level's index", under the sentence "the **collapse** rule is the column type" — and **collapse** is a bold term defined at 92-95 as "the distribution becomes one category" with 63-64 adding "nothing probabilistic survives"; a noul float column stores `distribution.to_f`, which by line 46 is the whole Bernoulli, and a score float column stores the expectation, which line 139 says is derived, not a category. The gem's own code and README already treat float as not-a-collapse: writing.rb:95/109 write the mass/expectation, staging.rb:256 calls the audit's argmax "the collapse the column lost", declarations.rb:965-972 raises "a score on a float column keeps the expectation, not the level; add an s1_answers column so the lens reads the stored distribution's collapse", and README:91 says "float keeps it · boolean / integer / string collapse it". The reader consequence is concrete: the sequenced-field bullet (286-288) says "that field's collapse enters the later state as a lens", so a reader who took the float column as the collapse would expect the stored float to be the lens value, whereas the code refuses and reads a category from s1_answers. The proposed split matches what the code does.

Not refutable. THEORY.md defines collapse as "the distribution becomes one category" and a category as a value where "nothing probabilistic survives", then files "a float keeps the mass" under "the collapse rule is the column type" (277-279) and generalizes "writing the answer into the row is the collapse" (296-297) — but the write path stores `distribution.to_f` for float columns (writing.rb:95,109), which is the Bernoulli's entire distribution for a judge and a summary of it for a score, never a category. The code itself treats the float column as a non-collapse: `s1_verify_predecessor_readable!` refuses `after:` a float score column without `s1_answers` because it "keeps the expectation, not the level", and `stored_collapse` calls the argmax "the collapse the column lost", so the reader consequence is concrete (a theory-following reader expects the row to hold a category and be usable as a sequenced predecessor; the gem raises). The theory's own sibling-column bullet lists `_probability` as "one part of the distribution," which is exactly what a float judge column stores — the proposed "sibling, not a collapse" framing matches the code. The README even separates the cases ("float keeps it · boolean / integer / string collapse it", README:91) while the source-of-truth text lumps them; the word "keeps" hints but does not resolve the contradiction under the theory's own terminology discipline.

claim: confident? and undecided? are said to read the distribution's entropy; in code neither does.
evidence: 54: "a thing with entropy (... how undecided it is, which is what `confident?` and `undecided?` read off)". 170: confident?(at) compares the provider's confidence scalar. 223 / answer.rb:51: undecided? is `(probability - threshold).abs < margin` — distance from a tunable threshold, not entropy (which is symmetric about 0.5). Probe: noul p=0.7 t=0.6 confident?(0.8)=false; choice confidence=1.0 confident?(0.8)=true.
proposal: Delete the parenthetical at 54, or replace with "(the theory's reason to keep it; the code reads confidence and threshold-distance, not entropy)".
reasons: Line 54's relative clause binds to "how undecided it is" (the ordinary-English gloss), not to "entropy"; it lists information theory's name for the object, and the sentence's only claim about the methods is that they read the distribution's undecidedness — which holds: `undecided?` is that by name and by its bold dictionary definition ("within a margin of the threshold", THEORY.md:223), and `confident?` reads either the noul's threshold-distance (169) or the provider's confidence, which the provider contract derives from the distribution's shape (cua: the argmax mass). The precise semantics the claim wants are already in the governing text — bold **confidence**/**threshold**/**undecided?** entries (166-177, 223) "mean only what [the dictionary] says", and answer.rb:37-39 documents the rejected symmetric-about-0.5 form — so no reader following the theory's own rule is led to expect an entropy computation. Probe: at the default threshold 0.5 a noul's `undecided?(m)` is exactly an entropy level-set (p=0.6 H=0.971 undecided, p=0.7 H=0.881 not), so the divergence exists only at non-default thresholds, where 169/223 already govern. The claim's own probe shows only that noul `confident?` takes a margin and choice/score take an `at` — which 170-171 and README:470-478 state outright. The proposal is a wording preference with no reader consequence.

Not refuted. The gloss at THEORY.md:54 binds `confident?`/`undecided?` to entropy ("how undecided it is"), but the code computes no entropy anywhere (grep: the word appears only at line 53), and the theory's own entries at 169-171 and 223 define them as threshold-distance and a provider scalar — so the inconsistency is real and internal, not merely loose wording. Probe shows the two notions diverge, not just differ in name: Noul p=0.5 (maximal entropy) at threshold 0.9 → `confident?(0.1)` is true, while p=0.85 at the same threshold → `undecided?(0.1)` is true; a flat Choice {0.34,0.33,0.33} with nil confidence → `confident?(0.99)` is true (distribution.rb:29), and Choice/Score have no `undecided?` at all. Reader consequence follows from line 3 ("where they disagree, the code is wrong"): a reader trusting line 54 could conclude the code is defective for not reading the distribution's spread, or expect `undecided?` on nominal/ordinal answers. The proposal (delete or reword the parenthetical to match 169-171/223) is the correct fix.

claim: Measured columns are declared "never evidence", yet a sequenced field puts an earlier measured column's collapse into the state as a lens.
evidence: 195-197: "the default form is its attributes less what is never evidence — ... every measured column with its siblings: a measurement is not its own evidence." 286-288: "that field's collapse enters the later state as a **lens**, `{ kind: "new_case" }`". 105: lens is "evidence added to the state". So `kind` is stripped as never-evidence, then re-added as evidence.
proposal: Reword 195: "less what is never the record's own evidence — ...; a measured column re-enters only by declaration, as the lens of a sequenced field (`after:`)."
reasons: The tension is real and the code confirms both halves: `Model.s1_omitted` strips every measured column from the default form (probe: facts = {transcript, urgent, urgent_probability}, `kind` gone), and a sequenced field's `state_for`/`sequenced` puts that same column's collapse back as a lens key (probe: request state = { this: …, kind: "new_case" }), while THEORY.md:105 and :253 define the lens as evidence. The only softening in the theory is the trailing clause "a measurement is not its own evidence," which scopes the rationale to the same question — but the rule it justifies ("every measured column," "never") is broader than that rationale, since `kind` is stripped from `case_type`'s form too, and the theory nowhere says measured columns re-enter by declaration. That is a reader consequence, not taste: the Form entry alone tells a reader an earlier verdict cannot be shown to a later question, and only :286 corrects it. One correction to the proposal, though: `after:` is not the only re-entry — a `given:` Proc reading the column re-adds it under any key with no sequencing (probe: `given: -> { { prior_kind: kind } }` → state `{ this: …, prior_kind: "other" }`), so the reword should say "never the form's evidence; it re-enters only as a lens — by `after:`, or by a lens that reads it."

The claim conflates the form with the state. THEORY.md:195-197 scopes "never evidence" to "the default form" — the rendering of the particular that sits at `this:` — and gives the reason as circularity ("a measurement is not its own evidence"; README:194-196 spells it out: "so a re-measure never shows the model its last verdict"). THEORY.md:105-107 defines the lens as a separate slot beside `this:` (`{ this: evidence, qualifications: … }`), evidence "to judge against" that "makes the judgement relative" — categorically not the record's own evidence, and by definition added. THEORY.md:286-288 says the earlier collapse "enters the later state as a lens", i.e. through exactly that declared, separate channel, and the code matches (staging.rb:213 merges `sequenced(batch, collapses)` into the lens, never into the form; README:313 forbids a form or call lens from naming `kind:`). Nothing is stripped and then re-added: `kind` never appears in the form and appears only beside it, as a standard for a different question — the proposed rewording restates what the lens definition and 286-288 already say.

claim: Rendering's codomain is given as the state in one place and as the facts (state minus lens) in another, so prepare is one arrow doing two jobs the dictionary splits inconsistently.
evidence: 100: "Rendering — the function from evidence to state". 69: "Prepare — fixes its rendering and attaches its lens" (so rendering alone does not reach the state). 215-216: "facts — the evidence as rendered, alone: what sits at `this` under a lens". state.rb: `@facts = Rendering.render(evidence); @lens = Rendering.render(given || {}); @rendered = ... { this: @facts, **@lens }`.
proposal: 100: "the function from evidence to facts — what is shown, in what shape. The state is the facts with the lens beside them; rendering the lens is the same function applied to it."
reasons: The text uses "the evidence as rendered" for the facts in three places (line 40: `{ this: <rendered evidence>, **lens }`; line 69: prepare "fixes its rendering and attaches its lens" as two steps; line 215: facts are "the evidence as rendered, alone") and once for the state (line 100: rendering is "the function from evidence to state"), so a bold term the document says "means only what it says" has two codomains that differ whenever a lens is present. The code sides with 69/215: `Rendering.render(evidence)` is assigned to `@facts`, the lens is rendered separately by the same function, and the composition `{ this: @facts, **@lens }` happens in `State#initialize`, not in `Rendering` (rendering.rb's own header comment repeats the line-100 wording and is wrong in the same way). The only escape reading — the lens is itself evidence (line 106), so rendering all evidence yields the state — fails because 106 says the lens is "added to the state", i.e. it enters after rendering, and 69 would then be redundant. The consequence is concrete: a reader following 100 expects `Rendering.render(x)` to be the state and it is not. Not refuted; the proposal's wording matches what the code does.

Not refuted. THEORY.md:100 gives Rendering the codomain "state", but the dictionary's own definitions make that hold only when there is no lens: line 69 says prepare "fixes its rendering and attaches its lens" (two steps, so the rendering alone is not yet the state), lines 34-40 define State as the rendering *with its lens attached* (`{ this: <rendered evidence>, **lens }`), and line 215 defines facts as "the evidence as rendered, alone" — i.e. the rendering's output is the facts, not the state. The code confirms it: `Rendering.render(evidence)` is assigned to `@facts` and the state is assembled in `State#initialize` (state.rb:72-75); a probe shows `Rendering.render("x") == state.facts` but `!= state.rendered` under a lens, equal only lensless. Line 106's "evidence added to the state" cannot rescue it, since that reading uses "state" for the pre-lens rendering while the State entry uses it for the post-lens whole — the same word for two objects, which is exactly the inconsistency claimed. Reader consequence is real: nothing in the theory says the lens is itself rendered (and so also subject to omission), which the code does (`Rendering.render(given)`) and the proposed wording would make explicit.

claim: Criteria and lens are said to attach to "different positions", but the question is not a position.
evidence: 244: "they attach to different positions: Criteria attach to the question ... The lens attaches to the state." 15: "Four positions" — evidence, state, distribution, category (27-64). Question is under "Concepts" (116).
proposal: 244: "they attach to different things: criteria to the question, the lens to the state."
reasons: THEORY.md fixes "positions" as structural vocabulary: line 15 "Four positions, three arrows", the `### Positions` section (26-64) enumerating only evidence/state/distribution/category, and line 301 "the four positions and the three arrows". Question is defined under `### Concepts` (97ff) and the Measure arrow treats it as an input ("the categories and the concept arrive with the question"), so it is neither a position nor an arrow. Line 245's "in exactly two places, and they attach to different positions" then names the question as one of the positions, contradicting the enumeration the reader just received; the deliberate shift from "places" to "positions" signals the term, not loose English. Not a bold-term violation, but a real inconsistency with reader consequence; the proposed "different things" fixes it.

Not refuted. THEORY.md uses "position" as a structural term for exactly the four diagram nodes: line 15 ("Four positions, three arrows"), the dictionary heading "### Positions" at line 26 listing only Evidence/State/Distribution/Category, and line 301 ("The gem owns the four positions and the three arrows"). Question is defined under "### Concepts" (line 116) and sits on the measure arrow ("by a question", line 12), so it is neither a position nor an arrow. Line 245 ("they attach to different positions: Criteria attach to the question") therefore contradicts the theory's own structural vocabulary; the sentence already says "two places", so "positions" is not a redundancy-free ordinary-English synonym there, and a reader who learned the four positions will look for which one the question is. The word is not bold, but the inconsistency is in a load-bearing structural term with a real reader consequence, and the proposed one-word fix ("different things") removes it.

claim: A predicate is defined as an unapplied question, but it carries a lens (given:) and a threshold — things the theory says attach to the state and the collapse, not the question.
evidence: 183: "Predicate — a question not yet applied to a state." 249: "The lens attaches to the state." predicate.rb:66: `question_options = ... options.except(*STATE_OPTIONS, :threshold)` — the predicate holds STATE_OPTIONS (given, provider, model, threshold) and re-applies them per element. README.md:772: `ψ.is?("qualified…", given: { qualifications: })`.
proposal: 183: "Predicate — a question, with the lens and collapse rule it will be applied under, not yet applied to a state; applying it prepares each element under that lens, then measures."
reasons: The claim conflates where a value is held with where it attaches: the theory says the lens "attaches to the state" (249) and the code does exactly that at application — `Predicate#measure` builds the state per element and then calls `state.given(**options[:given])` (predicate.rb:44-45, state.rb:101), so the lens never attaches to the question; likewise `threshold` reaches only `distribution.collapse(...)` on the `?` forms (predicate.rb:55, 66), matching "per-call" at 177 and "a `?` a boolean" at 186. The theory already tells the reader this: its code spelling for a predicate is `ψ.judge(…)` (185), and ψ is the prepare arrow that "fixes its rendering and attaches its lens" (69-70) — so a predicate is by construction a deferred prepare-then-measure(-then-collapse), and `given:`/`as:` are ψ's arguments, not the question's. A predicate with a lens is still "not yet applied to a state" because per 40 no state exists without `this`; the lens alone is not a state. The evidence also misreads STATE_OPTIONS (it is `%i[given as]`, not `given, provider, model, threshold`); the code's split-by-side is the theory's two-adjustments rule made mechanical, not a violation of it. The proposed rewording is a longer restatement of what 185 + 69 + 177 already say, with no reader consequence — README 761-772 and the predicate.rb header state the split explicitly.

Not refuted. THEORY.md:116-120 defines a question as `{ instructions, criteria }` and 249 puts the lens on the state, yet `Predicate#measure` (predicate.rb:44-46) takes raw evidence, prepares it under `as:`, attaches `options[:given]` as the lens, and only then measures — spec/s1/predicate_spec.rb:67-73 confirms the per-element state arrives as `{ this: …, topic: "billing" }` from a lens the predicate held. The code's own comment (predicate.rb:32-34) says the predicate's options split across state side (`given:`, `as:`), question side, and collapse side (`threshold:`), so the predicate is deferred prepare→measure→collapse, not "a question," and it is applied to evidence, not to "a state" as 183/258 say. THEORY.md never mentions this (only README:856 does), and the omission lands on the theory's own most-emphasized boundary (252-254): a reader taking 183 literally sees `given:` on a "question" and reads the lens as attached to the question. The claim's detail that STATE_OPTIONS includes provider/model/threshold is wrong (it is `%i[given as]`; threshold sits under COLLAPSES), but that does not rescue the definition.

claim: "Measurement" and "measure" (noun) are undefined and used for the product — a third and fourth name for what the dictionary calls the distribution — while 86-88 uses "measurement" for the act.
evidence: 86-88: "measurement (measurement theory: a point on a scale ...)" — the act. 177: "a measurement carries the threshold"; 233: "stored with the measurement"; 283: "`measurement(:col)` ... rebuilds the stored distribution"; 296: "the collapse of a measurement" — the product. 155: "makes the distribution a *measure*"; 263: "once each element is a measure"; 191: "per-element measures".
proposal: Add a dictionary entry: "**Measurement** — the product of one measure: the distribution together with the question, scale, threshold and confidence it was taken under; what a row stores and `measurement(:col)` rebuilds." Replace noun "measure" at 155/191/263 with "distribution".
reasons: Half the claim is refutable: "measurement" as the result of measuring is ordinary English polysemy that THEORY.md:5-6 licenses for every non-bold word, and the text already practises it with the bold term "judgement" (act at 111, "the product of a judgement" at 43), so 177/233/290/293 read unambiguously in context. The other half stands: noun "measure" at 155 (italicised, the document's convention for the gem's own names), 191 and 263 has no sense in the dictionary, whose only **Measure** entry is the act (73-76, 310), so a reader applying the text's own rule gets "calibration makes the distribution an act" at 155 and must fall back to an undefined measure-theoretic reading. In the Rails section "measurement" is also load-bearing for a thing that is neither the act nor the bare distribution (the s1_answers entry — distribution plus scale, threshold, confidence, digest; cf. audit.rb:5 "the whole measurement", README:121), which 283-284 describes but never names, so the proposed dictionary entry fixes a real gap rather than taste. One correction to the proposal: replacing *measure* at 155 with "distribution" yields the tautology "makes the distribution a distribution"; 155 needs a rephrase, 191/263 can take "distribution" since 261-262 applies all four operations to distributions.

THEORY.md:5-6 sets the standard the claim must be judged by: only bold terms are jargon, everything else is ordinary English — and "measurement" is never bolded, so it is the ordinary-English nominalization that names both the act and its result (exactly as the text uses "judgement" at 43 vs 154, "collapse" at 92 vs 293, "rendering" at 35 vs 99), which is standard polysemy, not two undefined terms. The result sense denotes precisely the bold **Distribution**: the diagram at line 11 says measure yields a distribution, 86-87 already glosses the measurement-theory word as "a point on a scale, here as a distribution over it", and the code confirms it — `measurement(:col)` (typesafe-rails lib/s1/measurable.rb:154) returns an `S1::Answer::Noul`/`Choice`/`Score` (an `S1::Distribution`, Noul carrying `threshold`), so every product use at 177/233/283/290/293 resolves to the object the reader already has a term for, and none can be read as the act (an act is not stored, rebuilt or collapsed). The Distribution entry at 48-54 explicitly lists five other-discipline names and calls "each true", so a multiplicity of names for this object is the theory's stated position, not a violation of it; the proposed bold **Measurement** entry would add a second jargon name for the same object — the very redundancy the claim objects to. Finally the proposal breaks 155: "*measure*" there is the probability-theory sense italicized like *posterior*/*credence* at 49-54 (calibration is what makes the numbers a genuine probability measure rather than "a label with a decoration"), and replacing it with "distribution" yields "makes the distribution a distribution", erasing the point of the axiom. No reader can draw a wrong inference about theory or code from any cited line, so the residue is taste.

location: THEORY.md:319-330 vs lib/s1/question.rb:124,131; lib/s1/answer.rb:107; lib/s1/result.rb:64-66; lib/s1/state.rb:96-107,131

(one).
proposal: Scope the rule at 319 to "the question-asking methods on a state and a predicate", and add a declared-exceptions line: "`collapse`, `given`, `with`, `to_s1` are not question methods; on the batch builder the verbs and their aliases add a question and return the builder; `Score#score` is the expectation (legacy alias)." Or drop the `choice`/`noul` aliases on Questions.
reasons: Three of the five evidence items are already addressed and fall away: `collapse` (THEORY.md:315), `given`/`against` (105, 216) and `to_s1` (224) have their own dictionary entries and are not measuring verbs (`given`/`against`/`with` are not verbs at all), and `ask`→measure / `ask?`→judge? are both declared at 322 and 327. The residual survives: THEORY.md:319 states "the rule for methods" without scope and 312/323 define `score` as the act and `choice` as "the category picked", yet the code the dictionary names ships `Questions#choice` (≡ `choose`, returns the builder, so `q.choice :d` yields an `Answer::Choice` in the Result where `state.choice` yields a Symbol — probe confirmed), `Answer::Score#score` (a Float expectation), and `Result#choices`/`scores` (kind filters returning distributions) — none declared in THEORY.md or README, only in spec/s1/aliases_spec.rb as "pre-theory spellings". The proposal (scope the rule to state/predicate question methods; declare the aliases or drop them) is a one-line fix, but the gap is genuine, so not refuted.

Partly refutable but the core stands. Refuted parts: `collapse`, `given`, `with`, `to_s1` are defined separately (THEORY.md:105,224,315; the rule at 319 says "a verb measures", which none of them do), and `ask`/`ask?` are both declared as aliases at 321-327, so those are not undeclared exceptions. Surviving parts, confirmed by probe: `Questions#choice(:d,"x",a:"A",b:"B")` returns `S1::Questions`, contradicting 324-325's stated identity "`x.choice(q,…)` is `x.choose(q,…).collapse` (a Symbol)"; `Answer::Score#score` is `alias score expectation` returning `1.0 (Float)`, while 312/321 name `score` a verb that returns the distribution; `Result#choices` returns `Answer::Choice` distributions although 324 says `choice` names the category. claim: `State#evidence` returns the rendered facts, not the evidence as the position defines it.

claim: The dictionary says confidence is 'gated by an explicit confident?(at), which is true when the provider reports none', but a noul's confident? takes a margin, not an 'at', and is false for exactly the cases the dictionary says are true.

claim: '& as joint probability' is licensed by calibration alone only if the two properties are statistically independent given the state; the code multiplies unconditionally and its comment claims 'the model guarantees it', conflating the provider's computational independence (each question scored without seeing the others) with independence of the events.
evidence: Probe: p1='about billing?'=0.9, p2='about a charge?'=0.9 -> (p1 & p2)=0.81, (p1 | p2)=0.99. For two near-synonymous properties the true joint is ~0.9, not 0.81. answer.rb:53: 'Distributions from one measure are independent (the model guarantees it), so these are exact for them'. THEORY.md:84 'the answers are independent of one another' describes the provider contract (jev: 'questions in a request are independent'), which is about scoring, not about the world.
proposal: THEORY.md:156: '`&` and `|` as the product/complement-product — exact when the two properties are independent given the state, a bound otherwise'. THEORY.md:84: 'the answers are computed independently of one another (no question sees another's answer); this is not statistical independence of what they measure.' Fix the answer.rb:53 comment to match.
reasons: Not refuted: the product rule at answer.rb:58-59 requires statistical independence of the two properties given the state, and calibration (THEORY.md:154, a per-marginal frequency guarantee) does not supply it; the derived 0.81 for two near-synonymous properties is itself miscalibrated by the theory's own axiom, since among such conjunctions ~90% are true. The text nowhere addresses the gap — README.md:400-403 makes the conflation explicit ("the model answers each question as if it were the only one … Independence is what makes `&`/`|` on the results exact"), and its flagship example `r[:is_lead] & r[:qualified]` composes two positively correlated properties then routes on `viable >= 0.85`, so the reader consequence is concrete misrouting. The provider contract (jev "questions in a request are independent", state.rb:19 "independent distributions") only asserts that no answer is context for another, which is computational, not a claim about the joint frequency of the events. One correction to the proposal: the product is not "a bound otherwise" — it sits strictly inside the Fréchet bounds max(0, p+q−1) ≤ P(A∧B) ≤ min(p, q), understating for positively correlated properties and overstating for negatively correlated ones, so the fix should say "exact under conditional independence; otherwise neither exact nor a bound, only the max-entropy joint consistent with the marginals."

Not refuted. Calibration is a marginal property (THEORY.md:154, "among such judgements, seven in ten are true") and cannot by itself make a product a joint: probe `a & a` on a 0.9 noul returns 0.81, but P(A ∧ A) = 0.9 — the identical question batched twice is computationally independent yet maximally dependent as an event, so "the model guarantees it" (answer.rb:53) is false on its face. The conflation is explicit and repeated, not incidental: README.md:401-403 defines Independence as "the model answers each question as if it were the only one … Independence is what makes `&`/`|` on the results exact", and README.md:675 says the gem "relies on that". Reader consequence is concrete: the README's own `viable = r[:is_lead] & r[:qualified] & ~r[:prior_rep]` (0.84) is routed against `0.85..`, and those properties are correlated, so the product lands on the wrong side of the threshold in exactly the direction the theory promised was exact. One caveat on the proposal, not the claim: the product is not "a bound otherwise" — the true joint sits anywhere in the Fréchet interval [max(0,p+q−1), min(p,q)], above the product for positively correlated properties and below it for negatively correlated ones.

claim: categories_shaped? turns any Hash with two or more String/nil values into candidates, so a record rendered as fields is silently measured as a choose over its field names — the theory says only 'a list of labels, or label → description' is candidates-shaped and that records take categories:.
evidence: Probe: { ticket: 'Refund my order', customer: 'Ann Lee' }.choose('Which team?') -> scale=[:ticket, :customer], collapse=:ticket. No error; the wire question asks the model to pick between 'ticket' and 'customer'. Without the inference the same call raises 'choice needs at least 2 options (got 0)' (question.rb:32) — the inference converts a loud error into a silent wrong question.
proposal: Either narrow the inference to Arrays of Strings and Hashes whose values are all nil or all Strings and whose keys are not Symbols (a record renders with Symbol keys; candidates are label => description with String labels), or document the rule in the dictionary exactly as coded: 'a Hash of two or more String-or-nil values is taken as candidates, whatever it was meant to be'.
reasons: Probe confirms the evidence exactly: `S1::State.new({ ticket: "Refund my order", customer: "Ann Lee" }).choose("Which team?")` puts `criteria: {"ticket"=>"Refund my order","customer"=>"Ann Lee"}` on the wire and collapses to :ticket, while the same Hash with a nested value raises "at least 2" — so the inference is purely structural (state.rb:229) and any two-string-field record is a choose over its field names. THEORY.md:148-151 and README.md:860 gate the inference semantically ("when the particular is itself the set of candidates") and never state the structural rule, so the text does not address it. The authors evidently know the two shapes are indistinguishable: typesafe-rails/lib/s1/measurable/state.rb:204 overrides `categories_shaped?` with the comment "A record's form is its fields, never the candidates" — a fix that exists only where the code knows it holds a record, leaving the core gem's plain-Hash case unguarded. The consequence is real, not taste: a loud ValidationError becomes a paid provider call answering a question nobody asked. (One caveat on the proposal, not the claim: the Symbol-key heuristic would not protect Rails `attributes`, which are String-keyed, and the spec's own candidate examples at state_spec.rb:500/521 are String-keyed too — the honest fix is either the rails-style opt-out or documenting the rule as coded.)

claim: 'a measurement carries the threshold it was taken under' is false in the default case: a noul with no explicit threshold reads S1.config.threshold at collapse time, so changing config after measuring changes the verdict.
evidence: Probe: measured under config 0.5 -> n2.threshold=0.5 collapse=true; config set to 0.95 afterwards -> n2.threshold=0.95 collapse=false. Client#measure calls with_threshold(nil) which stores nil (answer.rb:27), and Noul#threshold = @threshold || S1.config.threshold.
proposal: Either Client#measure stamps `threshold || S1.config.threshold` at measure time (making the dictionary true), or THEORY.md:177 says 'carries the threshold it was taken under when one was given; otherwise the config's, read at collapse'.

claim: 'compares by rank' holds only with the Level on the left; with a plain label on the left the comparison is String's, and Comparable's == is by text while <=> is by rank.
evidence: Probe on scale Cosmetic<Degraded<Blocking, lvl='Blocking'(rank 2): lvl >= 'Degraded' = true but 'Degraded' <= lvl = false; [lvl, 'Degraded'].max -> 'Degraded'. Two Levels with the same text and different ranks: a == b = true, (a <=> b) = 1, a.eql?(b) = true. level.rb:13-14 comment admits the left-side rule; the dictionary does not.
proposal: THEORY.md:181: 'compares by rank when it is the receiver (a label on the left compares as text; keep the level on the left, or compare Levels with Levels); == is String equality on the label'. Or define Level#== to compare rank when the other is a Level.
reasons: The left-side rule is already in the text: README.md:369-370 ("Put the level on the left… `"Broken…" <= lvl` is String's own compare, by alphabet") and the README dictionary at README.md:865 ("keep it on the left of a comparison with a label"), plus the lib/s1/level.rb:13-14 comment — so the evidence "the dictionary does not" is false. THEORY.md:181 describes the Level's own `<=>` (lib/s1/level.rb:34-40), which does compare by rank; a plain String receiver dispatching to String#<=> is Ruby's dispatch, not a Level comparing, and the same holds for every class that defines `<=>`. The `==` behaviour is deliberate and spec-pinned (spec/s1/level_spec.rb:74-102: equals its label and its index, Hash-key interchangeable with the label, `eql?`/`hash` by label; `==` is String's, not Comparable's, which the claim misattributes). Within one scale label and rank are bijective, so `==` and `<=>` never disagree; the probe's disagreement needs two Levels from different scales, where the theory defines no ordering (a rank is a position on *a* scale) and `<=>` is already meaningless. The proposal to make Level#== rank-based for Level-vs-Level would split `==` from `eql?`/`hash` and break the label-keyed Hash/pattern-match semantics the README and spec commit to.

Partly addressed, partly not. The left-side rule is already stated three times — README §Level lines 369–371 ("`"Broken…" <= lvl` is String's own compare"), README dictionary row 865 ("keep it on the left of a comparison with a label"), and level.rb:13–14 — so "the dictionary does not" is false for README's dictionary and only true of THEORY.md's one-line gloss; and the `==`-by-text point is deliberate and spec'd (level_spec 74–102: equals its label, Hash-key interchangeable), diverging from `<=>` only for same-text Levels on different scales, a comparison the theory never defines (also it is String#==, not Comparable's). What survives is the probe I reproduced: `[lvl, "Degraded"].max` → "Degraded" and `[lvl, "Degraded"].min` → "Blocking" on scale Cosmetic<Degraded<Blocking with lvl="Blocking", because Array#max/min make the later element the receiver, so the documented "keep the level on the left" rule cannot be followed and gives a silent wrong answer; likewise `lo.clamp("Degraded", "Blocking")` raises because Comparable compares the two label bounds as Strings. No text (THEORY, README, or code comment) covers that, and THEORY.md:181 carries no caveat at all; the claim's "or compare Levels with Levels" is the rule that actually holds, and the fix belongs in README's caveat and row 865 as much as in THEORY.md:181.

claim: The theory equates ψ(x) with S1::State.new(x), but they diverge when x already prepares itself: State.new(state, given:) nests the old state under a new `this`, while ψ(state, given:) merges the lens.

Rendering.render(state) takes state.to_s1.rendered (the whole, lens included) as the facts; per-state options of a to_s1 object (a record's provider/threshold) are also dropped by State.new and kept by to_state.
proposal: THEORY.md:71: Code line becomes 'ψ(x) = S1.to_state(x) (x.to_s1 when x answers it, else S1::State.new(x))'; drop 'S1::State.new(x)' as an equivalent, or make State.new(evidence) delegate to to_state when evidence responds to to_s1 so the two spellings agree.

Probe confirms the divergence on both gems: for a Ticket record with measured_against, S1::State.new(t, given: {z: 1}).rendered = {this: {this: {body: "b"}, policy: "30 days"}, z: 1} with options [] , while S1.to_state(t, given: {z: 1}).rendered = {this: {body: "b"}, policy: "30 days", z: 1} with options [:owner, :form]; so an instruction written "per `policy`" and cost attribution via owner both break under the State.new spelling. Probe confirms every fact: Rendering.render(result) and State.new(result).rendered yield "#<S1::Result:0x…>", a lensed { prior: result } carries that string beside `this`, and Result.instance_method(:to_h) == instance_method(:collapse). claim: The theory says entropy is 'what confident? and undecided? read off'; neither method reads entropy — one reads the provider's confidence scalar, the other the distance of one mass from a threshold.
evidence: distribution.rb:31: confident?(at) = confidence.nil? || confidence >= at. answer.rb:51: undecided?(margin) = (probability - threshold).abs < margin. No entropy is computed anywhere in lib.
proposal: Reword THEORY.md:54: 'a thing with entropy (information theory — how undecided it is; the code approximates this with the provider's confidence on nominal/ordinal scales and distance from the threshold on the dichotomous one)'.
reasons: Not refuted. `undecided?` measures proximity to the decision threshold, and that tracks Bernoulli entropy only when the threshold is 0.5: probed with threshold 0.9, p=0.85 (entropy 0.61 bits) reads undecided while p=0.50 (entropy 1.0, the maximum) reads decided — the opposite ordering from entropy. `Distribution#confident?(at)` never consults the mass at all: a near-uniform Choice ({x:.34,y:.33,z:.33}) with `confidence: nil` returns `confident?(0.99) == true`, and the cua provider's confidence is the top mass (cua.rb:49), which also is not entropy and even contradicts THEORY.md:168's "distinct from the mass on the winning category". The Confidence entry (THEORY.md:166-171) documents the real mechanisms, so 53-54's "which is what confident? and undecided? read off" is an internal inconsistency with reader consequence (a reader may expect a mass-derived fallback when a provider omits confidence, or expect undecided? to track uncertainty rather than boundary distance); by the theory's own "code is wrong where they disagree" standard this must be resolved, and the proposed rewording is a fair fix.

Not refuted. THEORY.md:53-54 says entropy is "what `confident?` and `undecided?` read off", but no entropy is computed anywhere in lib, and the methods observably diverge from it: a noul at p=0.5 (max entropy, H=1.0) under threshold 0.8 is `undecided?(0.1)=false`, while p=0.8 (H=0.72) is `undecided?=true` — the code reads distance from the threshold, which is not a function of entropy once the threshold leaves 0.5 (answer.rb:51, and the comment there explicitly rejects the 0.5-symmetric form). For nominal/ordinal, `confident?(at)` reads a provider scalar: cua.rb:49 sets it to the argmax mass (not entropy), and a near-uniform choice with nil confidence is `confident?(0.99)=true` (distribution.rb:31). THEORY.md:166-171 and README:470-476 already describe the real mechanism (provider estimate; distance from threshold), so lines 53-54 are internally inconsistent with the theory's own Confidence entry rather than "already addressed", and under the theory's "code is wrong where they disagree" rule a literal reader would conclude the code should compute entropy. The proposed reword is accurate and resolves it.

evidence: Probe: (ψ 'x').judge('q?', threshold: 0.7) -> ArgumentError 'threshold: only applies to a collapse (judge?, is?, same_as?)'; (ψ 'x').measure(threshold: 0.7) { … } -> same; S1.measure('x', {a: …}, threshold: 0.7) -> accepted, result.threshold=0.7.
proposal: THEORY.md:177: 'config, per-state (State.new(x, threshold:)), or per-collapse (judge?(threshold:), collapse(t)); a verb never takes one'. Either drop threshold: from Client#measure or list it as the plumbing exception.

The glossary row (THEORY.md:864) listing judge?("…", threshold: 0.9) and README 529–532 pin the intended meaning to the collapse, but that only shows the line 177 wording diverges from the theory's own resolution; it does not address the accepted Client-door keyword. Not false, not fully addressed, and a reader following line 177 hits an ArgumentError — so the claim stands.

Probe reproduces the evidence exactly: `(ψ 'x').judge('q?', threshold: 0.7)` and `(ψ 'x').measure(threshold: 0.7){…}` raise THRESHOLD_ON_VERB, while `S1.measure('x', qs, threshold: 0.7)` returns a noul stamped 0.7 (lib/s1/client.rb:13,28); the rails State (typesafe-rails lib/s1/measurable/state.rb:70,216) follows the State rule, so Client is the lone outlier. claim: Questions#choice is an alias of the verb choose, so in the batch builder the noun `choice` builds a distribution-yielding question — violating the rule that a noun names the collapsed thing, which the same word obeys on State, Primitives and Predicates.

proposal: Delete `alias choice choose` on Questions (keep noul, which is the wire name and a distribution name, not a collapse), or add the exception to THEORY.md:319.
reasons: The "leftover, not a pattern" premise is false: the builder's method set is exactly {judge|noul, choose|choice, score} — the theory verbs plus the three wire kind names that Question#type emits ("noul"/"choice"/"score", question.rb:23-51; THEORY.md:225 lists them as the wire names), and `level` is absent precisely because it is not a wire kind; spec/s1/state_spec.rb:530 titles this as deliberate. The noun rule at THEORY.md:319 governs measuring receivers ("a verb measures and returns the distribution"; README:249 "On every state", state.rb:32 "On a State"), and a Questions builder measures nothing and returns itself, so `q.choice` neither returns a distribution nor breaks the `x.choice == x.choose.collapse` identity. The inconsistency stands: THEORY.md:324-326 defines `choice` as the category picked (a Symbol) and says the nominal distribution has no proper name, yet `Questions#choice` (question.rb:131, mirrored at typesafe-rails lib/s1/measurable/questions.rb:45) declares a question whose batch answer is an `Answer::Choice` distribution — state_spec.rb:533 has to call `.to_sym` on `measure { |q| q.choice :pick, … }[:pick]`, which is exactly the reader consequence. Neither THEORY.md nor README lists the builder as an exception; README's batch section shows only the verbs, so the alias is undocumented sugar that contradicts the settled noun. One part of the evidence is wrong: it is not a leftover — it is deliberate (question_spec.rb:156, state_spec.rb:528 "choice / noul as its aliases there") and the alias set {noul, choice, score} is exactly the three wire kind names, which is why `level` is absent — but THEORY.md:225 says wire names are the provider's, not the gem's vocabulary, so that rationale does not rescue the alias under the theory's own terminology standard. The proposal (delete the alias, or add the exception at THEORY.md:319) is the right shape.
